main.title: Me & My Katamari
main.subtitle: A whole world to roll up in the hands
main.summary: Me & My Katamari is Namco's PSP action-puzzle game, first released in Japan on 22 December 2005. The Prince returns to roll objects into an ever-growing ball, carrying the Katamari idea onto a handheld for the first time. Small items make the ball large enough to gather bigger ones, steadily changing the meaning of the surroundings. What first appears to be an obstacle can eventually become another part of the collection. The portable version keeps that transformation of scale while finding a different control arrangement for a machine without two analogue sticks.

cards.heading: A whole world to roll up in the hands
cards.text: Me & My Katamari is Namco's PSP action-puzzle game, first released in Japan on 22 December 2005. The Prince returns to roll objects into an ever-growing ball, carrying the Katamari idea onto a handheld for the first time. Small items make the ball large enough to gather bigger ones, steadily changing the meaning of the surroundings. What first appears to be an obstacle can eventually become another part of the collection. The portable version keeps that transformation of scale while finding a different control arrangement for a machine without two analogue sticks.

cards.heading: Make two sets of buttons move like two hands
cards.text: The directional pad and face buttons imitate the paired movement of the console games, with shoulder buttons helping execute tight turns. The North American release also offers use of the analogue nub for movement. Learning that arrangement is part of gaining control over a ball whose shape becomes less tidy as objects accumulate. Different times of day and seasons change the central continent across missions. The player returns to familiar surroundings with another target size or condition, discovering how the same place can support a different route through its objects.

cards.heading: Katamari moves beyond its original creator
cards.text: Shuhei Kurose and Yutaka Yoshida directed the project, the first Katamari produced without series creator Keita Takahashi. Its music brings together returning series composers, maintaining the playful atmosphere around the Prince's work. Local wireless multiplayer allows friends to visit islands and compete over collections. Western releases followed in 2006. It was also the last Katamari published by Namco before the company merged with Bandai. The handheld adaptation shows how a distinctive physical idea can survive a substantial change in controls when its essential pleasure remains easy to recognise.

main.title: Kingdom Hearts II
main.summary: Kingdom Hearts II is a 2005 action role-playing game developed and published by Square Enix in collaboration with Buena Vista Games for the PlayStation 2.

cards.heading: Sora returns on PlayStation 2
cards.text: Kingdom Hearts II is a 2005 action role-playing game developed and published by Square Enix in collaboration with Buena Vista Games for the PlayStation 2. The game is a sequel to Kingdom Hearts, and like the original game, combines characters and settings from Disney films with those of Square Enix's Final Fantasy series. An expanded re-release of the game featuring new and additional content, Kingdom Hearts II Final Mix, was released exclusively in Japan in March 2007. The Final Mix version of the game was later remastered in high definition and released globally as part of the Kingdom Hearts HD 2.5 Remix collection for the PlayStation 3, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, Windows, and Nintendo Switch.

cards.heading: Searching for friends and facing Organization XIII
cards.text: Kingdom Hearts II is the second main installment in the Kingdom Hearts series, and the third game overall, taking place one year after the events of Kingdom Hearts: Chain of Memories. Sora, the protagonist of the first two games, returns to search for his lost friends while battling the sinister Organization XIII, a group of antagonists previously introduced in Chain of Memories. Like previous games, Kingdom Hearts II features a large cast of characters from Disney and Square Enix properties.

cards.heading: Building on the first game
cards.text: Concepts for Kingdom Hearts II began during the end of development of Kingdom Hearts Final Mix, with the game entering full development in 2003 and being announced at Tokyo Game Show 2003. Most of the first game's development team returned, including director Tetsuya Nomura, with the game being developed concurrently with Chain of Memories. In developing Kingdom Hearts II, the development team sought to address user feedback from the first game, give the player more freedom and options in combat and present a deeper and more mature plot.

cards.heading: Reception and the Final Mix editions
cards.text: The game was released to a very positive reaction from critics; earning several awards upon release. Reviewers praised the visuals, soundtrack, voice acting, and emotional weight, but assessments of the gameplay and narrative were mixed. In both Japan and North America, it shipped more than one million copies within weeks of its release, with over four million worldwide by April 2007. It has been cited as one of the greatest video games of all time.

main.title: Dead or Alive 4
main.subtitle: A tournament enters another console generation
main.summary: Dead or Alive 4 is Team Ninja's Xbox 360 fighting game, released in Japan and North America on 29 December 2005. Helena Douglas attempts to confront corruption within DOATEC while the series' ninjas continue their struggle against the organisation. The story introduces new competitors before making them available elsewhere, connecting a familiar tournament structure to the expanding cast. The new console gives the fighters and arenas a more detailed presentation. Underneath it remains a quick contest of strikes, throws and defensive responses, where recognising an opponent's intention can matter as much as completing a combination.

cards.heading: A tournament enters another console generation
cards.text: Dead or Alive 4 is Team Ninja's Xbox 360 fighting game, released in Japan and North America on 29 December 2005. Helena Douglas attempts to confront corruption within DOATEC while the series' ninjas continue their struggle against the organisation. The story introduces new competitors before making them available elsewhere, connecting a familiar tournament structure to the expanding cast. The new console gives the fighters and arenas a more detailed presentation. Underneath it remains a quick contest of strikes, throws and defensive responses, where recognising an opponent's intention can matter as much as completing a combination.

cards.heading: Make the opponent change their answer
cards.text: The exchange between attacking, throwing and countering encourages the player to vary a pattern that has become predictable. Movement within the arena offers another way to alter the distance or approach, while the surroundings can carry an encounter beyond its initial position. A fighter's familiar actions have to work against a person who may now be expecting them. Learning therefore involves more than memorising a move list. It means noticing which responses the opponent favours and choosing an action that makes that habit less useful in the next exchange.

cards.heading: A fighting game meets the early Xbox 360 community
cards.text: Online features gave the new console's players a way to continue those contests beyond the living room. Tomonobu Itagaki directed alongside Katsunori Ehara and Hiroaki Matsui, with the game becoming his final Dead or Alive fighting release before leaving Tecmo. Reviews were generally favourable, and sales passed one million copies during 2006. Later backward compatibility brought it to Xbox One and Xbox Series systems. Its original place remains close to the Xbox 360's arrival, presenting a recognised fighting series as a demonstration of the new machine's character and online possibilities.
